items.title: Constantinople fell to Ottoman cannons in 1453

options.text: Ottoman Sultan Mehmed II besieged Constantinople from 6 April; massive Hungarian-built cannons breached the Theodosian walls; the city fell on 29 May 1453, ending the 1,123-year Eastern Roman Empire

items.reveal:
Mehmed II, aged 21, had artillery cast by Orban, a Hungarian engineer — including the Basilic, around 8 metres long, firing stone balls of around 270 kg. The walls of Theodosius (built 5th century) had held for a thousand years; gunpowder ended their effectiveness.

Emperor Constantine XI Palaiologos died in the fighting; his body was never identified. Around 7,000 Byzantine and Genoese defenders faced perhaps 80,000-150,000 Ottoman troops.

Mehmed converted Hagia Sophia into a mosque (it remained one until 1934, when Atatürk converted it to a museum; reconverted to a mosque in 2020). The fall pushed Greek scholars and texts west into Italy — fuel for the late Renaissance.
items.why: Military technology can end empires. The fall of Constantinople closes the medieval Mediterranean and marks a conventional boundary between medieval and early modern history.

items.title: Newton published the Principia in 1687

options.text: 'Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica' set out three laws of motion and the law of universal gravitation, deriving Kepler's planetary laws mathematically — uniting terrestrial and celestial physics
A defence of the Aristotelian universe
A treatise on biblical chronology only

items.reveal_title: Standing on the shoulders of giants
items.reveal:
The Principia was published in Latin in July 1687, funded by Edmond Halley after the Royal Society's stock of unsold fish books left it short of cash. Newton derived the inverse-square law of gravity, the three laws of motion, and applied them to planets, comets, the tides and the shape of the Earth.

Newton had developed calculus (his 'fluxions') in 1665-66 during the plague closure of Cambridge. He published Opticks in 1704 in English.

Newton became Master of the Mint in 1699, prosecuting counterfeiters. He served as President of the Royal Society from 1703 to 1727. His tomb is in Westminster Abbey.
items.why: Modern physics begins with one book. The unification of celestial and terrestrial mechanics in 1687 is the high-water mark of the Scientific Revolution — and remained the framework of physics until Einstein.

items.title: The Elizabethan Settlement (1559) was a deliberate compromise
items.claim: What did the Elizabethan Religious Settlement of 1559 establish?

options.text: Act of Supremacy (Elizabeth as 'Supreme Governor' — softer than 'Supreme Head'); Act of Uniformity (revised 1559 Prayer Book); Thirty-Nine Articles (1571 final) — a deliberately broad 'via media' between Catholic and Reformed

items.reveal:
Elizabeth's first Parliament (1559) produced the legislation by narrow margins — particularly the Act of Supremacy, opposed by all 18 surviving bishops from Mary's reign. The 1559 Prayer Book combined elements of Cranmer's 1549 and 1552 books, with deliberately ambiguous language on the Eucharist.

The Act of Uniformity required attendance at parish church on pain of fines. The Thirty-Nine Articles (1563, finalised 1571) defined Anglican doctrine. The Settlement was challenged by Puritans wanting further reform and by Catholic recusants.

Elizabeth reportedly said she would not 'open windows into men's souls' — outward conformity was required; private belief was largely left alone.
items.why: The Church of England's modern shape — episcopal, vernacular, broad — is a 1559 political compromise that became national habit over 45 years. One of the most successful exercises in deliberate ambiguity in European history.
